summary: No new orders: all three holdings are still inside the limits set when they were bought, and the $249 in cash stays put until Nvidia reports on Tuesday, now without a permanent chief executive, and while long-term interest rates are still climbing.
thesis:
The account is one day old. Yesterday's orders filled at the open: about $300 each in the S&P 500 fund SPY and the equal-weight fund RSP, $150 in the health care fund XLV, and $249 left in cash. At the end of 12 November the account was worth $995.61 against $996.46 for the benchmark; most of the gap is the cost of the three purchases.

What has happened since the last decision:

- Nvidia's chief executive resigned on Thursday morning after the reports that led to the board's investigation, and the finance chief is running the company for now. The shares fell as much as 14% at the open and ended the day down about 4%. Results are due on Tuesday 17 November. This is the event the last decision was partly waiting for, and it is not over: the company reports in two trading days with no permanent leader.
- Long-term interest rates rose again. The 10-year Treasury yield went from about 5% to roughly 5.1% on Thursday and was quoted near 5.16% on Friday morning, with oil higher after the President signalled no early end to the Iran war. Two Federal Reserve officials said more tightening is likely to be needed.
- Wholesale prices for October, published this morning, rose 0.3% against 0.4% expected, a slightly better number than feared, though the yearly rate is still 6.5%. Weekly jobless claims on Thursday were 200,000, a little above the 195,000 forecast and still low.
- The S&P 500 fell about 0.4% on Thursday. In early trading on Friday it was close to flat while the index of smaller companies was down more than 1.5%.

Each holding judged against what I wrote when I bought it:

1. SPY ended 12 November at $757.12. The condition for cutting it is a day ending below its 200-day average, now about $731.60. It is 3.5% above that. Keep.

2. RSP ended at $220.72, down 0.87% on the day against 0.35% for SPY, so it lost a little ground on its first day. The condition for moving it into SPY is a day ending below its 50-day average, now about $215, or trailing SPY by more than 3 percentage points over a month while technology recovers. Neither is close: it is 2.7% above the 50-day average and technology is still well below its own. The thing to watch is that rising long-term rates hurt smaller and more indebted companies most, which is why the small-company index is weak this morning, and RSP holds more of those than SPY does. One day of that does not break the idea. Keep.

3. XLV ended at $187.83, down 0.59% on the day and about 1.3% below what I paid. The conditions for selling are a fall of more than 8% from the purchase price, a day ending below the 50-day average (about $174.70), or a concrete policy change on drug prices or insurance. None has happened and I found no such policy news. Keep.

4. Cash, $249 (25%). The reason for holding it has become stronger in one respect and no weaker in any: Nvidia's leadership question has turned into an actual vacancy days before results, and rates moved up. The end date is unchanged: this money goes into the market no later than the first trading day after the Federal Reserve decision of 9 December, and sooner if Nvidia's results pass and SPY is back above its 50-day average (about $764.80).

I considered putting some of the cash to work in bank or consumer staples funds, which are holding up, and decided against it because RSP already holds them and nothing has changed since yesterday to make a fourth line worth the trading cost. I also considered trimming RSP because of the rate move; the plan says to sell when the reason for holding breaks, and it has not.

A note on timing: this was written after the stock market opened on Friday, later than intended, so any order placed now would have filled at Monday's open. That did not affect the decision, since there are no orders.
risks: If Nvidia's results on Tuesday are well received and technology rebounds, the benchmark will beat this account, which holds less technology and has a quarter in cash. If long-term interest rates keep rising, RSP is likely to fall more than SPY because it holds more smaller, rate-sensitive companies, and it could reach its 50-day average quickly. Health care has risen a long way and could give back several percent if money that sheltered there moves back to technology. Holding cash loses ground whenever the market simply rises. Prices here are from the end of 12 November plus early readings on 13 November, which can change by the end of the day.
